Suturing is an interesting method to use if you have a cut in your skin and are looking to close it with stitches.  In the past, it was widely used for this purpose, but is less common today because it’s quite time consuming and is an inexact process.  

When practicing suturing, you should remember the fundamental principle of “closure”.  Simply put, suturing means making the surface of the skin back into a closed loop, since the skin doesn’t have a “cuff”.  To close a cut in the skin, a surgeon makes a small tunnel with a stitch that penetrates the skin from the outer side.  After that, he or she must also attach the ends of the stitch together, which can take some time and requires skill.  Once the ends of the stitch are secure, the surgeon then creates a strong, larger stitch which runs diagonally, effectively closing the whole wound.

The way that this type of stitching is done in practice is by using a curved needle and thread, which is common in the past but isn’t used very often today.  You may hear references to “suturing with the diastasis” if this type of stitching is done.  But some of the newer, more advanced types of stitches are now used instead, and these are more popular.

There’s a number of methods you can try, which are called in the medical field as “suturing techniques”.  Here are some of the most popular ones:

-   Continuous, interrupted, and running sutures
-   Stapling, and both superficial and deep sutures
-   Single-layer suturing and two-layer suturing
-   End-to-end (end-to-end suturing)
-   Ring suturing
-   Elastic suturing

Each of these suturing techniques have pros and cons, and you may or may not find one better than another.  Which suturing technique to use is really based on the situation you’re in, and the type of injury you’ve sustained.  

Let’s assume you have a relatively shallow cut on your hand, a single layer, and a four-millimeter running suture.  In that case, here’s how it would work:

-   Put one end of the suture at the base of the cut, and the other end near the end of the cut.  (The “end” means the side opposite the cut).
-   Bring one needle through the skin from the outside (the “outer side”), and run it through the back of the skin near the beginning of the cut.  This means that you are attaching the end of the stitch to the skin from the outside, and then sewing through it and pulling it back inside, creating a tunnel.  Be careful not to tear the skin, and to keep the two ends of the suture at the same level.
-   Then, bring the other end of the stitch to the other side of the cut, and sew it through to the back side of the cut, again being careful not to tear the skin.  This means that you are sewing back through the tunnel you created in step one, but on the back side of the cut.
-   Finally, bring the ends of the stitch back to the front of the cut, and make sure they are as level as possible.  Then, pull the two ends of the stitch tighter together by inserting a needle into one of the ends, and pulling the other needle tight to the first one.  Finally, tie off the ends of the stitch with some fishing twine or some other strong thread.

If you’re looking for an “ideal” suture method, I would use a running stitch to close the wound.  The length of your wound might make this more difficult, though, so you might want to look into other alternatives if you have a smaller wound.
